example: Inputs: Age 25 years, Resting Heart Rate 65 bpm. Step 1: maximum heart rate = 220 − 25 = 195 bpm. Step 2: heart rate reserve = 195 − 65 = 130 bpm. Step 3: Zone 2 (Fat Burn) = 65 + 60% of 130 to 65 + 70% of 130 = 143 to 156 bpm. Final result: max heart rate 195 bpm, with zones 130–143 (Recovery), 143–156 (Fat Burn), 156–169 (Cardio), and 169–182 (Peak). This is a general fitness guide, not medical advice.

faqs.a: For most adults it is roughly 60 to 100 beats per minute. Trained athletes are often lower, around 40 to 60. A single reading outside this range is not a diagnosis — check with a doctor if you are concerned.
faqs.q: What is a normal resting heart rate?

faqs.a: Zone 2 is labelled Fat Burn because a higher share of the energy comes from fat at that intensity. But total calories burned also matter, and higher zones burn more calories overall.
faqs.q: Which zone burns the most fat?

faqs.a: It is a widely used estimate, not an exact figure for any one person. Your true maximum can differ by 10 to 15 beats. Treat the zones as a guide.

formula: Maximum heart rate = 220 − age. Heart rate reserve = maximum heart rate − resting heart rate. Zone 1 (Recovery): resting + 50–60% of reserve. Zone 2 (Fat Burn): resting + 60–70%. Zone 3 (Cardio): resting + 70–80%. Zone 4 (Peak): resting + 80–90%.
howTo: Enter your age in the Age (years) field, for example 25.
Enter your resting heart rate in the Resting Heart Rate (bpm) field — measure it in the morning before getting up.
Tap Calculate to see your maximum heart rate.
Read the four training zones shown under the result.
Use a watch or fitness band during exercise to stay inside your chosen zone.
intro: The Heart Rate Calculator works out your maximum heart rate from your age and splits it into training zones, using the Karvonen method with your resting heart rate.
mistakes: Using 220 minus age as an exact personal maximum — it is a population average and can be off by 10 or more beats.
Skipping the resting heart rate and using rough zones that do not fit your fitness level.
Training in Zone 4 every session, which leads to exhaustion instead of fitness.
Measuring resting heart rate after coffee or a walk, which inflates it.
tips: Measure resting heart rate first thing in the morning, lying still, for three days and average the readings.
Beginners should spend most training time in Zones 1 and 2 before adding Zone 3 and 4 work.
Warm up for 5 to 10 minutes before reaching your target zone.
Stop and rest if you feel dizzy, chest pain, or unusual breathlessness — and seek medical help if it continues.
If you have a heart condition or take heart medicine, ask your doctor which zones are safe for you.
uses: It is used to plan exercise intensity: training in the right zone for recovery, fat burning, cardio fitness, or peak effort, instead of guessing how hard to push.
